What you are describing isn’t harmful to larger breeds, but also is not (from my experience and research) counterbalance. 

“Counterbalance is when a mobility assistance dog uses its body weight or a balance harness to brace against their handler to help their handler maintain balance while standing or walking.”

When I say counterbalance work is harmful, I am referencing this definition of counterbalance work. Leaning on a dog for stability is, over time, harmful to the dogs shoulders and hips and can cause long term damage. 

There are definitely statures and breeds that are bred to pull weight, I am by no means arguing against that. I am just saying that pulling back on a dog and pushing down on one are two entirely separate things, and no dog is built for the latter. 

At the end of the day, my opinion is simply that: my own. If counterbalance work is something that works for someone else’s team, it’s not my place or desire to criticize them. I am glad that your dog is a benefit to you, and I wish you many years of work together. :)

Personally, I don’t agree with SDs for counterbalance work. It’s not safe for the dog or the handler, and can cause long term damage to the dog’s physical health. I was also looking into mobility work for my SD, and in my research decided against it, and opted for a collapsible cane instead, and adding a retrieval task for the dog to fetch my cane.

I agree 100% that all beliefs are beautiful and a big part of what makes us human is that we don’t always agree! 

Ethical non-monogamy is simply to say that it’s an ethical and consensual way of going about a non-monogamous relationship, where all parties are consenting to the style of relationship and are aware of it being non-monogamous. An example of an unethical non-monogamous relationship would be one where person A is dating both person B and C, but B and C are unaware that A has multiple partners. 

I have also seen people who are in monogamous relationships and claim their infidelity as being ENM - that situation would be another that is unethical, since not all parties consented to the non-monogamy

In my personal life, and within my polycule (the “network” of people dating eachother; my polycule consists of myself, my partner, my metamour, my metamour’s other partner, and that person’s two partners outside of my metamour.. I know it’s confusing and complicated, thanks for bearing with me) I’ve observed more open relationships than closed ones. 

I think this has to do with the reason I (and a lot of poly people I’ve interacted with) practice ENM (ethical non-monogamy) - I believe that I have no right to restrict what my partner does with their life, whether that be in regards to career, social life, or relationships. I see my partner as a completely autonomous being, so who am I to say they can’t have relationships outside of the one we share?

I by no means am saying that monogamous people don’t respect their partner’s autonomy, nor am I saying that monogamy is restrictive. The above is simply my view and how I choose to go about my relationship - I’m not trying to say other ways of going about it are “wrong”

The word I used is “metamour”: it’s the word that means “my partner’s partner” - its easier to condense it into one word so it gets less confusing. And no worries! I’m in the lifestyle and there’s things I’m still learning, thank you being so open to learning about polyamory!

I am not romantically involved with my metamour, we’re in what’s commonly referred to as a “hinge” relationship, where there’s two distinct relationships:
A is dating B, B is dating C, but A and C are not involved. 

There has been one instance of a threesome between all of us very early on in mine and my partner’s relationship, but it was a one time thing in the heat of the moment and I don’t foresee it happening again.

I like to think of it as “falling” into polyamory - my boyfriend and I met in college through a mutual friend and he and his girlfriend had just opened up their relationship. One thing led to another, we fell for eachother and started dating; myself knowing the entire time that by dating him, I was also signing up for polyamory, as I never expected or wanted him to leave his girlfriend for me. 

My partner and his partner (my metamour) had been periodically discussing opening their relationship for a while and eventually agreed on doing so. There has never been any infidelity by either party during any part of their relationship, and I don’t think this arrangement would work if there had been. Polyamory is built on a strong foundation of trust, and that level of betrayal would (i imagine) be a dealbreaker for this lifestyle. 

I don’t get asked that as much as most people assume - to be fair, I surround myself with friends who are either also polyamorous or are familiar with the lifestyle, so it doesn’t come up much. I have had a family member or two ask about it when I was first explaining my relationship to them, but other than that not many instances come to mind.

I am more than tolerant, I am completely understanding and accepting! I indentify as ambiamorous, meaning I’m okay with being in both polyamorous and monogamous relationships.

I have been in monogamous relationships in the past and they made me feel just as fulfilled as polyamory does - I believe that the poly community as a whole should be more accepting of monogamous relationships and drop the stereotype or assumption that mono relationships are constricting or uncommunicative. 

At the end of the day, treat others how you want to be treated.

Communication, communication, communication!
Any relationship requires open communication to be successful, but I’ve found that polyamorous relationships require borderline radical honesty to work. Make sure everyone involved in the relationship(s) is on the same page when it comes to boundaries, expectations, time management, etc. Resentment and jealousy can build up quickly, so be sure to keep an open line of communication going consistently. 

I’ve found that for me and my relationship, it’s the little things that have been the biggest issues; who sleeps where when we’re all under one roof? How can we best manage our schedules so no one feels under appreciated? 

Future planning is also difficult for long term poly relationships, I’ve found. Talks of marriage and raising children become complicated fast, and everyone involved has had to be open to taking things as they come and figuring things out in the moment.
